pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Digestion & Enzymes

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion):** "the tissues and organs of the human digestive system, including adaptations to function and how the digestive system digests food (enzymes simply as biological catalysts)."

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-7 / MS-LS1-3):** MS-LS1-7 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-7]"; digestion also sits within MS-LS1-3 (interacting subsystems). NGSS frames digestion as matter transformation rather than naming each organ. (US = matter-flow model; UK = named organs + enzymes.)

- **Operational details:** Children trace the journey of food from mouth to large intestine, naming each organ (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, plus the roles of liver/bile and pancreas) and its job. They distinguish PHYSICAL digestion (chewing, churning, bile emulsifying fat — increasing surface area) from CHEMICAL digestion (enzymes breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones), and explain enzymes simply as biological catalysts, naming where key ones are produced (salivary glands, stomach, small intestine/pancreas). The absorbed small molecules then pass into the blood. The move that matters is seeing digestion as a PROCESS that converts food you can't absorb into molecules you can — breaking big into small.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on the KS2 digestive-system overview and cells-to-organ-systems hierarchy; feeds gut bacteria, diffusion-based absorption, and respiration substrate supply. A child is secure when they can follow food through the tract, say what happens at each organ, and explain why enzymes are needed (big molecules can't be absorbed).
bestPractices: Teach digestion as an ordered PROCESS (follow the food) rather than a static labelled diagram, so organ roles are seen in sequence and context.
Explicitly separate physical from chemical digestion, and show how physical breakdown (and bile) increases surface area to speed enzyme action.
Make the PURPOSE of chemical digestion concrete: big insoluble molecules cannot be absorbed until enzymes cut them small and soluble.
Keep enzymes 'simply as biological catalysts' per the KS3 boundary — avoid lock-and-key detail or rates work here.
Name where key enzymes are made (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas/small intestine) tied to where they act.
keyRepresentations: Labelled digestive-tract diagram with organ functions
'Follow the food' sequence from mouth to large intestine
Big-molecule → small-molecule breakdown schematic at each enzyme site
Villus close-up showing absorption of small molecules into blood
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the stomach does most digestion and absorption (the small intestine does most).
Believing food is 'inside the body' once swallowed, rather than passing through a tube until absorbed.
Confusing physical and chemical digestion, or thinking chewing alone is 'digestion'.
Thinking enzymes are alive, or are 'used up' in one reaction (they are catalysts, reused).
Assuming big molecules can be absorbed directly without being broken down.

learn.summary: Digestion for ages 11–13: trace food from mouth to large intestine, name each organ and its role (including the liver making bile and the pancreas making enzymes), separate physical from chemical digestion, and explain enzymes simply as biological catalysts that cut large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. The central insight is that digestion is a time-ordered PROCESS converting food you cannot absorb into molecules you can — big into small. Includes a driveable 'follow the food' model, a labelled tract for naming organs, an enzyme-tasting investigation, and optional anatomy/question-answering extensions, with scaffold limits flagged.

activities.title: Follow your food: pilot a meal through the gut
feedback: If a learner tries to absorb a big molecule: 'It won't cross the gut wall yet — a big molecule is too large. An enzyme has to snip it into small soluble pieces first. That's why chemical digestion is needed.'

If chewing alone is called 'digestion': 'Chewing breaks food into smaller lumps and makes more surface for enzymes — but the molecules inside are still large. Enzymes must cut those molecules before absorption.'
If absorption is placed in the stomach: 'Most absorption happens in the small intestine across the villi; the large intestine mainly reclaims water.'

Reinforce enzyme and bile sources: 'Starch enzyme starts in the mouth, protein enzyme and acid act in the stomach, bile from the liver emulsifies fat, and enzymes from the pancreas/small intestine finish the job.'
activities.rationale: Teaching digestion as a causal, time-ordered process (rather than a static labelled diagram) lets organ roles be seen in sequence and makes the matter transformation explicit, matching the UK requirement to explain how the system digests food and the NGSS call to model how food is rearranged as matter moves through an organism. The 'try to absorb a big molecule' moment makes the purpose of chemical digestion concrete.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the tissues and organs of the human digestive system, including adaptations to function and how the digestive system digests food (enzymes simply as biological catalysts)'.
NGSS MS-LS1-7 asks students to '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-7].'

Digestion combines physical breakdown (chewing, churning, bile emulsification) with chemical breakdown by enzymes (biological catalysts) that convert large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones for absorption in the small intestine.
learnerActions: Drive a mouthful of food step by step along the tract: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.
At the mouth, trigger both actions: teeth chew (physical) AND saliva's starch enzyme (amylase) begins cutting starch (chemical).
In the stomach, trigger churning plus acid, and a protein-cutting enzyme (protease) starting to break down protein.

In the small intestine, release bile — made by the liver (stored in the gallbladder) — to break a fat blob into small droplets (physical, increasing surface area), then let enzymes from the pancreas and small intestine finish cutting molecules small.
Watch the now-tiny molecules cross the villi into the blood; see water reclaimed in the large intestine.
Try to push a big (undigested) food molecule straight through the gut wall — observe it will not pass until an enzyme has snipped it into small soluble pieces.
Point out where each key enzyme is made (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas/small intestine) and where it acts.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion is an ordered process that physically and chemically breaks food down; big insoluble molecules cannot be absorbed until enzymes cut them into small soluble ones. Physical breakdown (and bile) increases surface area so enzymes work faster.

activities.title: Name the tract: tappable labelled digestive system
feedback: On the stomach-absorption flap: 'The small intestine, with its villi and large surface area, does most absorption; the stomach mainly churns and starts protein digestion.'
If organ and function are mismatched: 'Re-check the job of this organ — follow the food's order to place it, and remember the liver makes bile while the pancreas makes enzymes.'
activities.rationale: A labelled, tappable tract is an efficient way to secure organ names and roles and to separate physical from chemical digestion. It supports the naming layer required by the UK standard. Note that a static tract shows structure and roles but does not itself show the breaking-down process unfolding, so it is paired with the process model.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the tissues and organs of the human digestive system, including adaptations to function and how the digestive system digests food (enzymes simply as biological catalysts)'.
learnerActions: Tap each organ along the tract and read its job: mouth (chewing + salivary amylase), oesophagus (carries food down), stomach → 'muscular bag; acid + protease begin protein digestion', liver → 'makes bile that emulsifies fat', pancreas → 'makes digestive enzymes', small intestine → 'enzymes finish digestion; small soluble molecules absorbed here', large intestine → 'reabsorbs water'.
Match each organ to its function and each key enzyme to where it is produced (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas/small intestine).
Use a lift-the-flap check: 'Does the stomach do most absorption?' → reveal 'No — the small intestine does.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each organ has a named role in sequence, including the liver (bile) and pancreas (enzymes); absorption happens mainly in the small intestine, not the stomach.

activities.title: The cracker that turns sweet: tasting enzyme action (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: If the learner says small pieces are 'digested' and ready to absorb: 'Even a tiny crumb still contains large starch and protein molecules. Enzymes must cut those into small soluble molecules before they can cross the gut wall.'
If enzymes are described as alive: 'Enzymes are protein catalysts — not living things. They speed up the breakdown reactions without being used up or eating anything.'

Target answer to reinforce: 'Large molecules are chemically broken by enzymes into small soluble molecules — starch into sugars (glucose), proteins into amino acids, fats into fatty acids and glycerol — which are then absorbed through the gut wall. Physical digestion just increases surface area for enzymes.'
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain tasting task gives a direct sensory experience of enzyme action, challenging the common 'digestion = breaking into pieces' misconception and the belief that enzymes are alive. Keeping enzymes 'simply as biological catalysts' respects the KS3 boundary (no lock-and-key or rates work here).
sourceClaims: Digestion combines physical breakdown (chewing, churning, bile emulsification) with chemical breakdown by enzymes (biological catalysts) that convert large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones for absorption in the small intestine.
learnerActions: Before chewing anything, PREDICT how the taste of a plain cream cracker will change if you chew it slowly and hold it in your mouth for a minute or two, and say why.
After allergy/food-safety checks, chew a plain cream cracker slowly and hold it in the mouth for a minute or two, paying attention to any change in taste.

Observe and record what you actually taste: many people notice a slight sweetness developing as salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars such as maltose, though how strong the effect is varies from person to person.
Explain what happened, distinguishing what teeth do (break into pieces) from what the enzyme does (cut molecules).

Discuss the probe questions: Why can't a tiny bread crumb pass straight into the blood as it is? What is the difference between what your teeth do and what an enzyme does? If enzymes aren't alive, how do they break food down? Where along the gut does most digested food cross into the blood, and why there?
activities.intendedInsight: Chemical digestion by an enzyme is a real, directly experienced event — not just breaking food into smaller pieces. Enzymes are catalysts, not living creatures.

activities.title: Sequence and sort: order, categorise, match
feedback: If physical and chemical are confused: 'Physical breakdown makes pieces/droplets and more surface area; chemical breakdown uses enzymes to cut the molecules themselves.'
If enzyme sites are mismatched: 'Amylase starts in the mouth, protease and acid in the stomach, and pancreatic/intestinal enzymes finish in the small intestine; bile comes from the liver.'
activities.rationale: Sequencing, categorising and matching are clean checks of the naming and classification layer. These are recognition and ordering tasks: they assess and consolidate classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation of why chemical digestion is needed — pair with the modelling and POE tasks for that.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the tissues and organs of the human digestive system, including adaptations to function and how the digestive system digests food (enzymes simply as biological catalysts)'.
learnerActions: Order the organs food passes through from mouth to large intestine.
Categorise examples as physical digestion (chewing, churning, bile emulsifying fat) or chemical digestion (enzymes cutting molecules).
Match each key enzyme to where it is produced and where it acts, and match bile to the liver.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and classification: the correct order of organs, the physical/chemical distinction, and enzyme/bile sites.

activities.title: Optional enrichment: fly through the gut and field questions
feedback: Connect anatomy to function: 'All those folds and villi massively increase surface area, so more small molecules can be absorbed quickly.'
Redirect to the model when needed: 'Good question — now let's see where that fits in the follow-the-food journey.'
activities.rationale: A 3D fly-through may convey the folded absorptive anatomy vividly, and a conversational wrap may field genuine curiosity; both are optional enrichments, since the ordered process and organ roles are learned through driving the model and the investigation. Efficacy relative to the 2D model is untested.
learnerActions: Take an optional 3D tour along the gut and zoom into a villus to appreciate the folded, large surface area that aids absorption.
Use an optional 'ask an expert' conversation to explore curiosity questions such as 'what happens when you are sick?'
activities.intendedInsight: Surface-area anatomy (villi) explains why the small intestine absorbs efficiently; curiosity questions extend engagement without replacing the core process work.

constraints: Keep enzymes 'simply as biological catalysts' per the KS3 boundary — avoid lock-and-key detail or enzyme-rate work at this level.
The labelled tappable tract secures organ names and roles but is static: it does not itself show the breaking-down process or enzyme action unfolding, so pair it with the process model.

Sequence/categorise/match items are recognition and ordering tasks; they consolidate and assess classification but do not elicit independent construction of the explanation for why chemical digestion is necessary.

The 3D gut tour and the 'ask an expert' conversation are optional enrichments, not required to meet the objective and not shown to be superior to the 2D model; the core process is captured in the 2D model.
Food is 'passing through' a tube until absorbed — address the misconception that swallowed food is already 'inside the body'.
Avoid overclaiming the stomach's role: most chemical digestion is finished and most absorption occurs in the small intestine; the large intestine mainly reabsorbs water.
Bile is an emulsifier/surfactant made by the liver, not an enzyme — treat bile emulsification as physical breakdown.
For the cracker tasting task, follow allergy/food-safety checks (e.g. gluten) before giving any food to learners.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The BBC Bitesize source (physical+chemical breakdown, large insoluble → small soluble, absorption in small intestine) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific claim as unverified pending review. The DfE and NGSS standards claims are marked verified.

Simplifications flagged for review: 'starch → glucose/sugars' in the target answer is a teaching simplification (salivary amylase's immediate product is maltose, later broken to glucose); acceptable at this level but noted. Fat digestion was corrected to 'fatty acids and glycerol' (the original listed only fatty acids); still a KS3-level simplification of lipid chemistry. Bile is an emulsifier/surfactant made by the liver, not an enzyme — kept as physical breakdown here, which is correct.
Enzyme/bile site attribution is simplified (salivary amylase, gastric protease, pancreatic/intestinal enzymes, liver-made bile); fine for KS3 but do not overstate exact locations.

assess.poeTask: Give each student a plain cream cracker and ask them to chew it slowly and hold it in the mouth for a minute or two. Ask them to PREDICT how the taste will change and why. It turns noticeably sweet as salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars — a direct experience of chemical digestion by an enzyme, challenging 'digestion is only breaking into pieces'.
probeDeeper: A crumb of bread is tiny — so why still can't it pass straight into the blood as it is?
What is the difference between what your teeth do and what an enzyme does to the food?
If enzymes aren't alive, how do they break the food down?
Where along the gut does most of the digested food actually cross into the blood, and why there?
assess.correctAnswer: Breaking food into small pieces (physical digestion) is not enough. The large molecules must be chemically broken down by enzymes into small, soluble molecules — starch into glucose, proteins into amino acids, fats into fatty acids — which can then be absorbed through the gut wall into the blood. Physical digestion just increases the surface area for enzymes to work on.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digestion just means breaking food into smaller and smaller pieces
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce molecular breakdown: even a tiny crumb still contains large starch and protein molecules; enzymes cut these into absorbable molecules.
errorPatterns.distractor: Once the food is in tiny pieces it's digested and can pass into the blood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says chewing and churning are all there is to digestion; a small enough piece can be absorbed

errorPatterns.pattern: Digestion happens only in the stomach
errorPatterns.nextMove: Map enzyme sites: amylase in the mouth, protease and acid in the stomach, and most digestion and absorption in the small intestine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes all digestion to the stomach, ignoring mouth and small intestine

errorPatterns.pattern: Enzymes are alive — tiny creatures that eat the food
errorPatterns.nextMove: Enzymes are protein catalysts, not alive; they speed up the breakdown reactions without being used up or 'eating' anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes enzymes as living organisms rather than molecules

errorPatterns.pattern: Nutrients are absorbed in the stomach; the intestines are just for waste
errorPatterns.nextMove: Most absorption is in the small intestine (villi, huge surface area); the large intestine reabsorbs water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places absorption in the stomach and treats the small intestine as merely a waste pipe

responseLevels.gap: Equates digestion with breaking food into smaller pieces; no notion of enzymes or molecular breakdown.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes physical from chemical digestion, explains enzymes break large molecules into small soluble ones for absorption in the small intestine, and names where key enzymes act.
responseLevels.partial: Knows enzymes are involved and can name some organs, but still says small pieces can be absorbed, or confines digestion/absorption to the stomach.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you chew bread it breaks into tiny pieces, and your stomach churns it smaller still. A student says 'that's digestion done — the food is now small enough to pass into the blood.' Is breaking food into small pieces enough? If not, what else has to happen to it before it can be absorbed?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands digestion distinguishes chemical breakdown of molecules by enzymes from merely breaking food into smaller lumps. A child who thinks 'small pieces = digested' misses that the molecules inside are still too big to absorb.
